title: Day 05 — Deposits, NS&I, Bonds & Fixed Interest Securities
subtitle: Ch2 Topics 1–8: Deposits · NS&I · Offshore Deposits · Money Market Instruments · Fixed Interest Securities · Government Gilts · Corporate Bonds · Local Authority Bonds
main_html:
Overview: Ch2 Topics 1–8

Exam FocusHigh-frequency areas

FSCS limit (£85,000 per firm), NS&I 100% security, Premium Bond max (£50,000), inverse price/yield relationship, gilts vs corporate bonds credit risk, index-linked gilt coupon linked to RPI

CeMAP 1Ch2 scope

Financial products underpinning savings, investment, and mortgage advice. Understanding risk/return trade-offs and tax treatment is essential for client suitability.

1. Deposits

Bank and building society deposits are the most common savings vehicle in the UK. They are simple, accessible, and protected by the FSCS up to £85,000 per person per authorised firm (£170,000 for joint accounts).

Account typeKey features
Instant accessWithdrawals on demand; lowest interest rate
Notice accountTypically 30/60/90 days notice to withdraw; higher rate
Fixed-rate bondFixed term (1–5 yr); higher rate; early access usually penalised
Regular savingsCommit to monthly deposits; promotional rate for 12 months
Current accountDay-to-day transactions; low or zero interest
Exam Trap: The FSCS protects £85,000 per authorised firm, not per account. If a client holds £100,000 in two accounts at the same bank (same authorisation), only £85,000 is protected. Two separate banks = £85,000 each.

2. National Savings and Investments (NS&I)

NS&I is a government-backed savings institution. All products are 100% secure — there is no FSCS limit because the UK government guarantees the full amount.

ProductKey facts
Premium BondsMin £25, max £50,000. Prizes instead of interest. Tax-free prizes. Prize fund rate varies. No interest earned.
Income BondsVariable rate, monthly interest paid to bank account. Min £500, max £1,000,000.
Direct SaverVariable rate, online only. Min £1, max £2,000,000.
Fixed Interest Savings CertificatesFixed rate, fixed term (1 or 2 year). Tax-free returns. Currently on sale periodically.
Index-Linked Savings CertificatesReturn linked to CPI + fixed %. Tax-free. Currently not on general sale.
Green Savings Bonds3-year fixed; funds UK government green projects; tax-free interest.
NS&I Direct ISACash ISA; variable rate; counts toward annual ISA allowance.
Key point: NS&I products are backed by HM Treasury. The savings limit on Premium Bonds is £50,000 per person. Prize payments are completely tax-free.

3. Offshore Deposits

Deposits held in jurisdictions outside the UK — most commonly the Channel Islands or Isle of Man.

  • Potential advantages: may offer higher interest rates; useful for internationally mobile clients
  • NOT covered by UK FSCS: protected only by the local compensation scheme (Channel Islands/IOM schemes offer limited cover)
  • Tax: UK residents must declare all offshore interest to HMRC — offshore â  tax-free. Interest accrues gross but must be declared on self-assessment
  • Currency risk: if account is in a foreign currency
  • Uses: legitimate tax deferral (not avoidance) where interest rolls up offshore and is declared when remitted; useful for non-domiciled individuals using remittance basis
Exam Trap: Offshore deposits are NOT tax-exempt for UK residents. The interest is taxable when received or credited. Do not confuse 'offshore' with 'tax-free'.

4. Money Market Instruments

Short-term debt instruments used by banks, governments, and large corporates to manage short-term funding. Typically mature within one year.

Treasury Bills (T-Bills)
  • Issued by UK government via DMO
  • Typically 91-day term
  • Issued at a discount to face value; no coupon
  • Return = difference between issue price and £100 face value
Certificates of Deposit (CDs)
  • Issued by banks acknowledging a deposit
  • Fixed term, fixed interest rate
  • Tradeable in secondary market — provides liquidity
Commercial Paper
  • Short-term unsecured corporate debt
  • Issued by large creditworthy companies
  • Issued at a discount; typically <270 days
Repos
  • Sale and repurchase agreement
  • Sell asset + agree to buy back at higher price later
  • Effectively a secured short-term loan
  • Used by BoE to implement monetary policy

5. Fixed Interest Securities

Bonds that pay a fixed coupon (regular interest payment) until the redemption date when the face value is repaid. Understanding yield is essential.

ConceptExplanation
Par value (nominal)Face value — typically £100. Bond redeemed at par unless otherwise stated.
CouponAnnual interest as a % of par (e.g., a '5% Treasury Gilt 2030' pays £5/year per £100 nominal)
Flat yield (running yield)Coupon Ã· market price Ã 100. Ignores capital gain/loss at redemption.
Redemption yield (yield to maturity)Total return including coupon AND capital gain/loss to redemption. The most complete measure.
Yield curvePlot of yields for different maturities. Normally upward sloping (longer = higher yield = more risk).
Critical Exam Point — Inverse Relationship: When market interest rates rise, existing bond prices FALL (and vice versa). If you hold a 3% bond and new bonds offer 5%, your bond is less attractive â its price falls. This is the most-tested fixed interest concept.

6. Government Gilts

UK government bonds issued by HM Treasury via the Debt Management Office (DMO). 'Gilt-edged' = very low default risk (sovereign risk only).

Conventional Gilts
  • Fixed coupon paid half-yearly
  • Redeemed at par on maturity date
  • Named by coupon & year: e.g., 4% Treasury Gilt 2032
  • Safest fixed interest investment
Index-Linked Gilts
  • Coupon AND redemption value linked to RPI
  • Protect against inflation (real return)
  • Real yield = nominal yield â inflation
  • Lower coupon than conventional gilts

Why gilts matter for mortgages: Swap rates (which determine fixed mortgage rates) are closely tied to gilt yields. When gilt yields rise, fixed mortgage rates tend to rise.

7. Corporate Bonds

Debt securities issued by companies to raise capital. Higher yield than gilts to compensate for credit risk.

  • Credit ratings: issued by S&P, Moody's, Fitch. Investment grade: BBBâ/Baa3 and above. Below = high-yield ('junk') bonds.
  • Debenture: corporate bond secured on the company's assets — lower risk than unsecured bonds
  • Subordinated bonds: lower ranking in insolvency — higher yield compensates for greater risk
  • Spread: extra yield over gilts = credit spread; reflects perceived default risk
Risk vs return: AAA corporate bond â lowest yield. CCC high-yield bond â highest yield but highest default risk. Gilts = benchmark (risk-free rate).

8. Local Authority Bonds

Bonds issued by UK local authorities (councils) to fund capital expenditure.

  • Slightly higher yield than equivalent gilts (local authorities cannot print money)
  • Considered very safe — backed by the local authority's power to levy council tax
  • Less liquid than gilts (smaller market)
  • Fixed term, fixed rate
  • Not covered by FSCS in the same way as bank deposits
  • Also issued via the Public Works Loan Board (PWLB) — local authorities borrow directly from central government

Memorise

FSCS Limits
  • Deposits: £85,000 per authorised firm
  • Joint accounts: £170,000
  • NS&I: 100% (no limit) — HM Treasury backed
  • FSCS does NOT cover investment losses in funds/shares
Bond Price/Yield Relationship
  • Rates rise â bond prices FALL
  • Rates fall â bond prices RISE
  • Flat yield = coupon Ã· price Ã 100
  • Redemption yield = most complete measure
NS&I Key Numbers
  • Premium Bonds max: £50,000
  • Premium Bonds min: £25
  • Prizes: totally tax-free
  • All NS&I: 100% secure
Gilts
  • Conventional: fixed coupon, redeemed at par
  • Index-linked: coupon + redemption linked to RPI
  • Gilt yields â influence fixed mortgage rates
  • DMO issues gilts on behalf of HM Treasury

Practice Questions

Q1. A client holds £120,000 in two current accounts at the same authorised bank — £60,000 in each account. How much is protected by the FSCS?
A. £120,000 — both accounts are covered separately
B. £85,000 — the FSCS limit applies per authorised firm, not per account
C. £60,000 — only the first account is covered
D. £170,000 — joint account rules apply
Reveal answer
Answer: B — £85,000. The FSCS limit of £85,000 applies per person per authorised firm. Even though the money is in two separate accounts, both are at the same firm. The £170,000 limit applies to joint accounts (shared between two people), not two separate single accounts at the same bank.
Q2. Market interest rates rise from 3% to 5%. What happens to the market price of an existing 3% conventional gilt?
A. It rises, because higher rates make all bonds more valuable
B. It remains unchanged — gilts are backed by the government
C. It falls, because newer bonds offer a higher return, making the existing gilt less attractive
D. It falls only if the gilt is index-linked
Reveal answer
Answer: C. This is the fundamental inverse price/yield relationship. When new bonds are issued at 5%, an existing bond paying only 3% must trade at a lower price so that its yield is competitive. Price and yield move in opposite directions. This is a core exam concept.
Q3. Which NS&I product pays prizes instead of interest, and what is the maximum investment allowed per person?
A. NS&I Income Bonds; maximum £1,000,000
B. NS&I Premium Bonds; maximum £50,000
C. NS&I Premium Bonds; maximum £25,000
D. NS&I Direct Saver; maximum £2,000,000
Reveal answer
Answer: B — NS&I Premium Bonds; maximum £50,000. Premium Bonds pay no interest. Instead, all potential interest is pooled into a prize fund and distributed as tax-free cash prizes. The minimum holding is £25 and the maximum is £50,000 per person. All NS&I products are 100% secure (no FSCS limit applies).

title: Day 06 — PIBS, Annuities, Shares, Derivatives & Structured Products
subtitle: Ch2 Topics 9–16: PIBS · Child Trust Fund · Help to Save · Annuities · Shares · Derivatives · Sharesave/Share Options · Structured Products
main_html:
Overview: Ch2 Topics 9–16

Exam FocusHigh-frequency areas

Help to Save bonus rate (50%), max £1,200 total bonus; Open Market Option for annuities; ordinary vs preference shares; derivatives: futures vs options; SAYE discount (up to 20%); structured products: capital-protected vs capital-at-risk

CeMAP 1Ch2 scope

Range of investment and income products from building society bonds to complex derivatives. Exam tests understanding of risk, tax treatment, and regulatory protections.

9. Permanent Interest Bearing Shares (PIBS)

Issued by building societies to raise capital. Despite the name, they function like bonds.

  • Fixed interest rate, paid regularly like a bond coupon
  • No maturity date — perpetual (hence 'permanent')
  • Traded on the London Stock Exchange
  • Subordinated: in a winding-up, PIBS holders rank below ordinary depositors — high credit risk
  • Price is very sensitive to interest rate movements (like long-dated bonds)
  • FSCS protection: the interest payments may be covered, but PIBS holders do NOT get FSCS protection for capital loss — they rank as creditors, not depositors
Exam Trap: PIBS are shares in name but behave like fixed interest securities. They are NOT protected by the FSCS against capital loss. Do not confuse them with ordinary building society savings accounts.

10. Child Trust Fund (CTF)

  • Government scheme — closed to new accounts since 2 January 2011
  • Replaced by Junior ISA for new savers
  • Existing CTF accounts continue and can be transferred to a Junior ISA
  • Initial government contributions: £250 for most children; £500 for lower-income families
  • Parents and family could contribute up to the annual limit
  • Funds locked until the child reaches age 18
  • Two types: Cash CTF or Stocks & Shares CTF
Key exam point: CTF is closed to new entrants. Junior ISA is its replacement. Existing CTF holders can transfer to a Junior ISA but cannot hold both simultaneously.

11. Government's Help to Save

Targeted savings account for people on low incomes claiming Universal Credit or Working Tax Credit.

FeatureDetail
EligibilityPeople claiming UC (with minimum earnings) or Working Tax Credit
Save£1–£50 per month
Term4 years total; can withdraw at 2 years or 4 years
Bonus — Year 250% of the highest balance reached in years 1–2. Max bonus: £600 (if max £1,200 saved).
Bonus — Year 450% of the increase in highest balance from year 2 to year 4. Max additional bonus: £600.
Total max bonus£1,200 (if £50/month saved throughout)
WithdrawalsAllowed, but reduce the highest balance for bonus calculation
Exam Trap: The bonus is calculated on the highest balance, not the balance at the end. Withdrawals reduce the highest balance and therefore the bonus — this is the key trap.

12. Annuities

An annuity converts a lump sum (typically a pension fund) into a guaranteed income. Once purchased, the decision is irreversible.

Types of Annuity
  • Level: fixed income throughout — eroded by inflation over time
  • Escalating: income increases each year (e.g., 3%/year fixed or RPI-linked)
  • With-profits: income varies with investment performance
  • Enhanced / impaired life: higher income for those with health conditions or lifestyle factors
  • Joint life: continues (at reduced rate) to surviving spouse/partner
Key Concepts
  • Open Market Option (OMO): right to buy an annuity from ANY provider, not just your existing pension provider. Essential to maximise income.
  • Annuity rate: affected by age, gender (now unisex), health, gilt yields, provider, type chosen
  • Guarantee period: annuity pays for minimum guaranteed period (e.g., 5/10 years) even if annuitant dies earlier
  • Capital protection: returns remaining fund value on death
Open Market Option is examinable: A client should always exercise the OMO — shopping around can significantly increase retirement income. Failure to advise the OMO is a major regulatory failing.

13. Shares

TypeDividendVotingLiquidation ranking
Ordinary sharesVariable; discretionaryYes (1 vote per share)Last (residual claim)
Preference sharesFixed rate; paid before ordinaryUsually noBefore ordinary shareholders
Cumulative preferenceUnpaid dividends accumulate and must be paid before any ordinary dividendUsually noBefore ordinary

Corporate Actions

  • Rights issue: company offers new shares to existing shareholders at a discount to market price — raises new capital
  • Bonus/scrip issue: free additional shares issued from reserves — no new cash raised; dilutes share price proportionally
  • Share buy-back: company repurchases own shares — reduces shares in issue, increases EPS
Limited liability: ordinary shareholders can only lose the amount they invested. Company debts cannot be claimed against personal assets (unlike sole trader/partnership).

14. Derivatives

Financial contracts whose value derives from an underlying asset (shares, currencies, commodities, interest rates).

Futures
  • Obligation to buy/sell the underlying asset at a set price on a future date
  • Binding on both parties
  • Used for hedging (protecting against price changes) or speculation
  • Traded on exchanges (standardised contracts)
Options
  • Right but not obligation to buy (call option) or sell (put option)
  • Buyer pays a premium for this right
  • Exercise price = strike price
  • American option: exercisable any time before expiry
  • European option: exercisable only at expiry
CFDs (Contracts for Difference)
  • Profit/loss = difference in asset price from open to close
  • No ownership of underlying asset
  • Margined product — leverage magnifies gains AND losses
  • Not suitable for most retail clients
Hedging vs Speculation
  • Hedging: using derivatives to reduce existing risk exposure
  • Speculation: using derivatives to take on risk for potential profit
  • Same instrument, opposite purpose
Exam Trap: Futures create an OBLIGATION; options give a RIGHT but no obligation. An option buyer's maximum loss is limited to the premium paid. A futures position has unlimited potential loss.

15. Sharesave and Share Option Schemes

SchemeKey features
SAYE (Sharesave)Save £5–£500/month for 3 or 5 years. Option to buy employer shares at up to 20% discount to market price at scheme start. At maturity: use savings to buy shares at option price OR take savings as cash. No income tax on the discount at purchase if HMRC-approved.
CSOP (Company Share Option Plan)Options to buy shares at market value. Limit: £60,000 of options per employee. No income tax on exercise if held for 3 years. CGT on eventual disposal.
EMI (Enterprise Management Incentives)For smaller companies. Up to £250,000 of options per employee. Very tax-efficient. Income tax and CGT advantages.
SIP (Share Incentive Plan)Free shares, partnership shares (bought from pre-tax salary), matching shares. Held in trust for minimum period.

16. Structured Products

Investment products whose return is linked to the performance of an underlying index (e.g., FTSE 100), with a defined term (typically 3–7 years).

Capital-Protected (PGPs)
  • Capital returned at maturity regardless of index performance
  • Plus potential upside (e.g., 100% of FTSE growth, capped)
  • Lower potential return for the protection
  • Protection only valid if held to maturity AND issuer doesn't default
Capital-at-Risk Products
  • Capital at risk if index falls below a defined barrier (e.g., 50% barrier)
  • Higher potential return to compensate
  • Kick-out plans: early maturity if index hits target on annual measurement date
Exam Traps: (1) Counterparty risk: if the issuing bank defaults, the investor could lose all capital even in a 'capital-protected' product. (2) Early exit: breaking the product before maturity usually incurs significant penalties. (3) Participation rate: if the product offers only 80% of index growth, the investor does not get the full gain.

Memorise

Help to Save — Bonus
  • Save £1–£50/month; 4-year term
  • 50% bonus on highest balance
  • Max total bonus: £1,200
  • Year 2 max bonus: £600; Year 4 max: £600 more
  • Eligible: UC (working) or WTC claimants
Shares Quick Reference
  • Ordinary: variable dividend, voting, last in liquidation
  • Preference: fixed dividend, usually no vote, ahead of ordinary
  • Rights issue: new shares at discount to existing holders
  • Bonus issue: free shares from reserves — no cash raised
Derivatives
  • Future = OBLIGATION to buy/sell
  • Option = RIGHT (not obligation) to buy/sell
  • Option buyer pays premium; max loss = premium
  • CFDs: margined, leverage, no asset ownership
Annuity Key Terms
  • OMO: right to shop around — always exercise
  • Enhanced annuity: better rate for health/lifestyle
  • Joint life: income continues to surviving spouse
  • Irreversible once purchased
  • Level annuity eroded by inflation

Practice Questions

Q1. Kezia is eligible for Help to Save. She saves the maximum £50/month for the full 4-year term without making any withdrawals. What is the total government bonus she will receive?
A. £600 — the bonus is only paid once at the end of year 4
B. £1,200 — 50% bonus paid in two stages based on highest balance
C. £1,440 — 60% bonus on total contributions of £2,400
D. £600 — 25% bonus paid at year 2 and 25% at year 4
Reveal answer
Answer: B — £1,200. Help to Save pays a 50% bonus at year 2 on the highest balance reached in years 1–2 (max £600 if balance = £1,200), and another 50% bonus at year 4 on the increase in highest balance from year 2 to year 4 (max further £600). Total max bonus = £1,200.
Q2. Which of the following best describes the difference between a futures contract and an options contract?
A. Futures can only be used for hedging; options can only be used for speculation
B. A futures contract creates an obligation to trade; an options contract gives the right but not the obligation to trade
C. Options are exchange-traded; futures are always over-the-counter
D. The maximum loss on a futures contract is limited to the initial margin
Reveal answer
Answer: B. This is the fundamental distinction. A futures contract is binding — both parties MUST complete the transaction at the agreed price and date. An options contract gives the buyer the right (not obligation) to buy (call) or sell (put) at the strike price; the buyer's maximum loss is the premium paid.
Q3. Mrs Tan is about to retire and convert her pension fund into an annuity with her existing pension provider. Her adviser must make her aware of what right?
A. The right to delay taking the annuity for up to 10 years
B. The Open Market Option — the right to purchase an annuity from any provider
C. The right to a tax-free lump sum of 100% of the fund
D. The right to a capital-guaranteed annuity at no extra cost
Reveal answer
Answer: B — the Open Market Option (OMO). Every individual with a defined contribution pension has the right to shop around and buy an annuity from any provider, not just their existing pension company. Failure to advise the OMO is a significant regulatory breach. Annuity rates vary significantly between providers, and enhanced annuities may offer much better income for those with health conditions.

title: Day 07 — EIS, VCTs, Stock Markets, Real Estate, REITs, ESG, FX & Unit Trusts
subtitle: Ch2 Topics 17–24: Enterprise Investment Schemes · VCTs · Stock Markets · Real Estate · REITs · ESG · Foreign Exchange · Unit Trusts
main_html:
Overview: Ch2 Topics 17–24

Exam FocusHigh-frequency areas

EIS: 30% income tax relief, 3-year hold, £1m limit; VCT: 30% relief, 5-year hold, £200k limit, tax-free dividends; REITs must distribute 90% of rental profit; PIDs taxed as property income (not dividends); unit trust: dual pricing, open-ended

CeMAP 1Ch2 scope

Tax-advantaged equity investments, property alternatives, and collective investment vehicles. EIS/VCT tax reliefs are frequently examined in conjunction with their risk profile.

17. Enterprise Investment Schemes (EIS)

Government scheme to encourage investment in smaller, higher-risk, unquoted trading companies. High risk — not suitable for most clients.

FeatureDetail
Income tax relief30% of amount invested, deducted from income tax bill. Max investment: £1,000,000/year (£2m for knowledge-intensive companies).
Minimum holding period3 years — if sold sooner, income tax relief is clawed back
CGT deferralA chargeable gain from any asset can be deferred by reinvesting in EIS shares within 1 year before or 3 years after the gain
CGT exemptionGains on EIS shares themselves are CGT-exempt if held â¥3 years AND income tax relief was claimed
Loss reliefLosses on EIS shares (net of income tax relief) can be offset against income or capital gains
Dividend incomeTaxable — no exemption on dividends from EIS companies
IHT Business ReliefEIS shares in qualifying trading companies: 100% relief from IHT after 2 years
Exam Trap: EIS income tax relief is 30%, not 20% or 40%. The £2m limit only applies to 'knowledge-intensive companies'. Dividends from EIS are taxable. The holding period for income tax relief is 3 years (vs VCT which is 5 years).

18. Venture Capital Trusts (VCTs)

Listed investment trusts that hold a portfolio of unquoted/AIM-listed companies. More diversified than EIS.

FeatureDetail
Income tax relief30% of amount invested. Max investment: £200,000/year.
Minimum holding period5 years — if sold sooner, income tax relief is clawed back
Dividend incomeTax-free — unlike EIS, VCT dividends are exempt from income tax
Capital gainsGains on VCT shares are CGT-exempt — no CGT on disposal of VCT shares
CGT deferralNOT available for VCTs — unlike EIS, no CGT deferral relief
IHTListed VCT shares do NOT qualify for Business Relief (they are listed)
EIS vs VCT — Key Differences
EISVCT
Max invest£1m£200k
Hold period3 years5 years
IT relief30%30%
DividendsTaxableTax-free
CGT deferralYesNo
Listed?NoYes
Both share:
  • 30% income tax relief
  • High risk — small/unquoted companies
  • Not suitable for mainstream clients
  • Need to be a qualifying new subscription

19. Stock Markets

Primary Market
  • Companies issue new shares to raise capital
  • IPO (Initial Public Offering): first-time listing
  • Rights issue: additional shares offered to existing holders
  • Proceeds go to the company
Secondary Market
  • Investors trade existing shares between each other
  • Proceeds go to the seller, NOT the company
  • Provides liquidity for shareholders
London Stock Exchange (LSE)
  • Main Market: large, established companies; stringent listing requirements; includes FTSE 100/250
  • AIM: Alternative Investment Market; smaller, growing companies; less regulation; higher risk; AIM shares can qualify for EIS/IHT relief
Market Mechanics
  • Market makers: quote bid (buy) and offer (sell) prices; provide liquidity
  • Bid/offer spread: market maker's profit
  • Settlement: T+2 (2 business days after trade)
  • SETS: electronic order book for FTSE stocks

20. Real Estate

Direct investment in physical property — the most tangible asset class.

Residential Property
  • Buy-to-let: rental income + capital gain potential
  • Higher SDLT: surcharge on second homes (3%)
  • Mortgage interest: limited tax relief for individuals (Section 24 — basic rate credit only)
  • CGT on disposal (minus PPR if ever lived in)
  • HMO (Houses in Multiple Occupation): higher rental yield, more regulation
Commercial Property
  • Offices, retail, industrial units
  • Typically long leases (5–25 years)
  • Yield usually higher than residential
  • More sensitive to economic cycles
  • VAT may apply on purchase/rental

Characteristics of direct property investment: illiquid (hard to sell quickly), high transaction costs (SDLT, legal fees, agent fees), needs management, undiversified, but provides rental income + inflation hedge over long term.

21. Real Estate Investment Trusts (REITs)

Listed companies that own income-producing real estate. Combines property exposure with stock market liquidity.

FeatureDetail
Distribution requirementMust distribute at least 90% of rental profits to shareholders each year
Tax exemptionExempt from corporation tax on qualifying rental profits and gains from property sales
Property Income Distributions (PIDs)Dividends from the ring-fenced rental profits. Taxed as property income (not dividends) — usually paid with 20% basic rate tax deducted at source
Non-PID dividendsFrom non-property activities — taxed as ordinary dividends
ISA/pension eligibleREIT shares can be held in an ISA or SIPP; within these wrappers PIDs receive gross treatment
ListingMust be listed on a recognised stock exchange (liquid, unlike direct property)
Exam Trap: REIT PIDs are taxed as property income, NOT dividend income. This means the dividend allowance does NOT apply to PIDs, and they are liable to income tax at the investor's marginal rate (after the 20% withheld at source credit).

22. ESG — Green Investing

ESG stands for Environmental, Social, and Governance. It integrates non-financial factors into investment decisions.

Environmental
  • Climate change & carbon emissions
  • Renewable energy use
  • Water management
  • Biodiversity impact
Social
  • Employee welfare and diversity
  • Supply chain ethics
  • Community relations
  • Human rights
Governance
  • Board diversity & independence
  • Executive pay transparency
  • Anti-corruption policies
  • Shareholder rights

Investment Approaches

  • Negative screening: exclude sectors (tobacco, weapons, fossil fuels, gambling)
  • Positive screening: invest in best-in-class ESG performers in each sector
  • ESG integration: incorporate ESG analysis into standard financial analysis
  • Impact investing: direct investment to achieve measurable positive outcomes
  • Stewardship/engagement: use shareholder influence to improve company ESG practices
Greenwashing: misleadingly portraying a product as more environmentally friendly than it is. A key regulatory concern — FCA has issued guidance on sustainability disclosure requirements (SDR).

23. Foreign Exchange

  • Spot rate: exchange rate for immediate (today) delivery of currency
  • Forward rate: agreed exchange rate for a future date — used to hedge currency risk (locks in a known rate)
  • Exchange rate quotation: £/$ = number of dollars per £1. If £/$= 1.26, £1 buys $1.26.
  • Sterling weakens: imports become more expensive (inflationary) â cost-push inflation pressure; exports become cheaper (competitive advantage)
  • Sterling strengthens: imports cheaper; exports more expensive (less competitive)

Factors affecting exchange rates

  • Interest rate differentials: higher rates attract foreign capital â stronger currency
  • Inflation: high inflation â currency depreciates relative to lower-inflation countries
  • Trade balance: surplus â demand for £ â stronger pound
  • Political stability and government policy
  • Speculation and market sentiment
Exam relevance: Currency risk applies to any overseas investment. A UK investor holding US equities gains if $ strengthens against £ and loses if $ weakens. Offshore accounts and EIS in overseas companies carry currency risk.

24. Unit Trusts

An authorised collective investment scheme — pools investors' money to invest in a diversified portfolio.

Structure
  • Open-ended: units created when investors buy; cancelled when they sell
  • Trustee: legal owner of assets; independent of fund manager
  • Fund manager: makes investment decisions under the trust deed
  • Regulated by FCA under COLL rules
Pricing
  • Dual pricing: manager quotes a higher offer price (buy) and lower bid price (sell)
  • Bid/offer spread = fund manager's initial charge
  • Price = NAV of underlying assets Ã· units, adjusted for charges
  • Dilution levy: sometimes charged to protect existing investors
Income Units vs Accumulation Units
  • Income units: income (dividends) distributed to unitholders
  • Accumulation units: income automatically reinvested â unit price rises
Charges
  • Initial charge (front-end load): e.g., up to 5%
  • Annual Management Charge (AMC): e.g., 0.75%/year
  • TER (Total Expense Ratio): all ongoing charges including AMC + admin
  • OCF (Ongoing Charges Figure): now preferred term

Memorise

EIS vs VCT Quick-Fire
  • Both: 30% income tax relief
  • EIS hold: 3 years; VCT hold: 5 years
  • EIS max: £1m; VCT max: £200k
  • EIS divs: taxable; VCT divs: tax-FREE
  • EIS CGT deferral: YES; VCT: NO
REITs
  • Must distribute â¥90% of rental profits
  • PIDs = property income (NOT dividends)
  • PIDs: 20% basic rate tax deducted at source
  • Exempt from corporation tax on rental profits
  • Can be held in ISA/SIPP
Unit Trusts
  • Open-ended; dual pricing (bid/offer)
  • Trustee â  fund manager (independent)
  • COLL rules; FCA authorised
  • Income units distribute; accumulation reinvest
ESG Approaches
  • Negative screen: exclude harmful sectors
  • Positive screen: best-in-class ESG picks
  • Integration: ESG + financial analysis
  • Impact: measurable positive outcomes
  • Greenwashing: misleading ESG claims

Practice Questions

Q1. An investor puts £50,000 into an EIS-qualifying company in 2024/25 and holds the shares for 4 years before selling at a gain. Which statement is correct?
A. The investor receives 40% income tax relief and the gain on disposal is fully taxable
B. The investor receives 30% income tax relief; dividends received are tax-free; the gain on disposal is CGT-exempt
C. The investor receives 30% income tax relief; dividends received are taxable; the gain on disposal is CGT-exempt (as held >3 years)
D. The investor receives 20% income tax relief; the full gain is subject to CGT at 10%
Reveal answer
Answer: C. EIS income tax relief is 30% (not 20% or 40%). Dividends from EIS companies are taxable as normal. However, gains on disposal of EIS shares are CGT-exempt provided the shares have been held for at least 3 years AND income tax relief was originally claimed. The holding period here (4 years) exceeds the minimum 3-year requirement.
Q2. A UK REIT pays a Property Income Distribution (PID) to an individual investor. How is this distribution taxed?
A. As dividend income — eligible for the dividend allowance
B. As property income — basic rate tax (20%) deducted at source; investor declares balance on self-assessment
C. As capital gain — taxed at 18% or 28% depending on total income
D. Tax-free — REITs are exempt from all UK taxes on distributions
Reveal answer
Answer: B. PIDs from REITs are classified as property income, NOT dividend income. This means the dividend allowance does not apply. The REIT deducts 20% basic rate tax at source. Higher-rate and additional-rate taxpayers declare the PID on self-assessment and pay the additional tax. Within an ISA or SIPP, PIDs are received gross and shelter entirely from tax.
Q3. Compared to investing directly in commercial property, which advantage do REIT shares specifically offer?
A. REITs are exempt from all income tax on distributions
B. REITs provide liquidity — shares can be bought and sold on the stock exchange
C. REITs are not subject to stock market volatility, unlike shares
D. REIT shares qualify for 100% IHT Business Relief after 2 years
Reveal answer
Answer: B — liquidity. Direct commercial property is illiquid — it can take months to buy or sell. REIT shares are listed on a stock exchange and can be traded throughout the day, providing much greater liquidity. Note: REITs can still experience volatility as listed companies (C is wrong). REITs pay income that is taxable (A is wrong). Listed REIT shares do NOT qualify for IHT Business Relief (D is wrong).

title: Day 08 — Investment Trusts, OEICs, ISAs, Endowments & Life Assurance
subtitle: Ch2 Topics 25–33: Non-Mainstream Pooled Investments · Investment Trusts · OEICs · ETFs & Platforms · ISAs · Endowment Assurance · Qualifying Policies · Investment Bonds · Term Life Assurance
main_html:
Overview: Ch2 Topics 25–33

Exam FocusHigh-frequency areas

Investment trusts: closed-ended, gearing, NAV vs discount/premium; ISA: £20,000 limit, LISA 25% bonus/25% penalty, Junior ISA £9,000; Investment bonds: 5% rule, chargeable events, top-slicing; qualifying policy: 10-year minimum term; term assurance types (level/decreasing)

CeMAP 1Ch2 scope

Collective investment structures, tax-efficient wrappers, and life assurance products. Heavily tested because of their relevance to financial planning, mortgage protection, and retirement saving.

25. Non-Mainstream Pooled Investments (NMPIs)

NMPIs are complex, unregulated or lightly regulated collective investment schemes not suitable for ordinary retail investors.

  • Examples: Unregulated Collective Investment Schemes (UCIs), traded life policy investments (TLPIs), some types of property funds, hedge funds, private equity funds
  • FCA restriction: NMPIs may only be promoted (marketed) to professional clients, sophisticated investors, or high-net-worth individuals
  • Key risks: illiquid, complex, opaque fee structures, no FSCS protection for investment losses, potentially high leverage
  • Standard retail clients cannot be recommended NMPIs through a standard financial promotion
Exam Trap: The NMPI marketing restriction means that advisers cannot simply recommend these products to any client. It is not just that they are unsuitable — there is a regulatory prohibition on promoting them to ordinary retail clients.

26. Investment Trusts

A closed-ended listed investment company. Unlike unit trusts/OEICs, the number of shares is fixed — you buy/sell existing shares on the stock exchange.

FeatureDetail
Closed-endedFixed number of shares in issue; new shares not routinely created to meet demand
ListedShares traded on London Stock Exchange throughout the day
GearingCan borrow money to invest — amplifies potential returns AND losses
NAV per share(Total assets â liabilities) Ã· shares in issue = intrinsic value per share
Discount to NAVShare price < NAV — common; investors buy £1 of assets for <£1
Premium to NAVShare price > NAV — less common; investors pay more than the assets are worth
GovernanceBoard of directors oversees the fund manager; regulated under Companies Act not COLL
Gearing effect: If an investment trust borrows 25% of its assets to invest, and the portfolio rises 10%, the equity return is amplified. However if the portfolio falls, losses are amplified too. Gearing = magnification of both gains AND losses.

27. Open-Ended Investment Companies (OEICs)

Similar to unit trusts but in company rather than trust form. Open-ended: shares created/cancelled as investors buy/sell.

Key Features
  • Single price: one price for buying AND selling (unlike dual-priced unit trusts)
  • Authorised Corporate Director (ACD) manages the OEIC
  • Depositary safeguards assets (equivalent of trustee)
  • FCA-authorised; COLL rules apply
  • Swing pricing may be used to prevent dilution of existing investors by large flows
Umbrella Funds
  • Single OEIC can contain multiple sub-funds (e.g., UK equity, bond, global)
  • Investor can switch between sub-funds — may be CGT event
  • Each sub-fund has different charges and risk profiles
  • Simplifies administration under one legal structure

Unit Trust vs OEIC comparison

Unit TrustOEIC
StructureTrustCompany
PricingDual (bid/offer)Single price
Manager titleFund ManagerACD
Asset custodianTrusteeDepositary
Multiple fundsNoYes (umbrella)

28. Exchange Traded Funds (ETFs) and Platforms

ETFs
  • Investment fund listed on a stock exchange — traded like a share throughout the day
  • Typically passive: tracks an index (e.g., FTSE 100, S&P 500)
  • Low costs — no active management fee; TER often 0.05%–0.3%
  • Diversified in one trade
  • Can be physical (holds actual assets) or synthetic (uses swaps/derivatives to replicate index)
  • Synthetic ETFs carry counterparty risk
  • Can be held in ISA or SIPP
Investment Platforms (Fund Supermarkets / Wrap Platforms)
  • Online services allowing investors to hold multiple products in one place
  • Examples: Hargreaves Lansdown, AJ Bell, Fidelity, Transact
  • Facilitate: fund selection, ISA/SIPP administration, portfolio reporting, switching between funds
  • Platform charges: may be a % of assets (e.g., 0.25%/year), flat fee, or per-transaction
  • Relevant for retail clients building a diversified portfolio efficiently

29. Individual Savings Accounts (ISAs)

Tax-efficient wrapper — income and gains within an ISA are completely exempt from UK income tax and CGT.

ISA typeKey features
Cash ISASavings deposits; interest tax-free; FSCS protection £85k applies
Stocks & Shares ISAInvest in funds, shares, bonds, ETFs, REITs; gains and income tax-free; FSCS does NOT cover investment losses
Innovative Finance ISAPeer-to-peer loans and crowdfunding; higher risk; FSCS does not cover investment losses
Lifetime ISA (LISA)Age 18–39 to open; 25% government bonus (max £1,000/year on £4,000 contribution); use for first home (property up to £450,000) or from age 60; 25% withdrawal penalty applies otherwise (loses bonus AND portion of own money effectively)
Junior ISAUnder 18; annual limit £9,000; cash or S&S; inaccessible until child reaches 18; can transfer from CTF
Annual ISA allowance 2024/25
  • Total: £20,000 per person
  • Can split across multiple ISA types
  • LISA contribution: counts toward the £20,000 (max £4,000 to LISA)
  • Junior ISA: separate £9,000 limit
  • Unused allowance cannot be carried forward
LISA Penalty Detail
  • Withdrawal penalty: 25% of withdrawal amount
  • Bonus was 25% of contribution — the 25% penalty on the grossed-up amount effectively claws back the bonus AND 6.25% of your own money
  • Penalty does NOT apply: first home purchase (up to £450k), terminal illness, death, or from age 60
Exam Trap: The LISA penalty is 25% of the withdrawal amount (not just the bonus). Because the bonus was added first (growing the pot), the 25% penalty on the larger amount exceeds the original bonus — the saver loses some of their own money if they withdraw early for an ineligible reason.

30. Endowment Assurance

A life assurance policy that also has a savings/investment element. Pays out either on death within the term OR at maturity (whichever comes first).

With-Profits Endowment
  • Invested in with-profits fund
  • Reversionary bonuses: declared annually, added to the sum assured — once added, cannot be taken away
  • Terminal bonus: discretionary lump sum added on maturity or death claim; can be substantial
  • Smoother returns than unit-linked; less volatile
Unit-Linked Endowment
  • Value linked directly to investment fund performance
  • Higher potential returns, more volatile
  • More transparent — you can see fund value daily
  • No reversionary bonuses
Low-Cost Endowment
  • Historically used to repay interest-only mortgages
  • Projected to repay the mortgage at maturity (but not guaranteed)
  • Many policies in 1990s-2000s suffered shortfalls as investment returns disappointed
  • No longer commonly sold as mortgage vehicles
Surrender & Paid-Up
  • Surrender value: cash received if policy cancelled early; likely less than premiums paid in early years
  • Paid-up policy: stop paying premiums; reduced sum assured maintained until maturity
  • Market value adjuster (MVA): with-profits fund may apply on early exit in poor market conditions

31. Qualifying Policies

Certain life assurance policies that meet HMRC's criteria are 'qualifying' — gains are exempt from income tax (and CGT) on maturity or surrender.

Requirements to qualify:

  • Regular premiums payable at least annually throughout the term
  • Minimum term: 10 years (or to age 75 if earlier)
  • Sum assured â¥ 75% of total premiums payable over the term (ensures life cover is genuine)
  • Cannot be a single-premium policy (those are investment bonds — non-qualifying)
  • Cannot be assigned for value (except on divorce settlement)
Tax treatment of qualifying policies: Any gain realised on maturity, surrender, or death claim is completely free of income tax and CGT for the policyholder. This is a significant advantage over investment bonds.
Endowment assurance policies are typically qualifying policies if they meet the above criteria. The qualifying status must be maintained — surrendering early may trigger a tax charge if HMRC's conditions weren't met throughout.

32. Investment Bonds

Single-premium, non-qualifying life assurance policies with an investment element. Commonly used for tax planning, especially by higher-rate taxpayers and those expecting to become lower-rate taxpayers in future.

FeatureDetail
5% withdrawal ruleUp to 5% of the original investment can be withdrawn each year without an immediate tax liability. Unused allowance accumulates (e.g., 3 years unused = 15% in year 4). Tax is deferred — not exempt.
Chargeable eventsDeath, full surrender, partial surrender exceeding 5% cumulative allowance, policy maturity, assignment for value. Trigger income tax assessment.
Gain calculationGain = surrender value + all withdrawals â premiums paid. Taxed as income at marginal rate.
Basic rate creditGains are treated as having had 20% basic rate tax paid. Basic rate taxpayers have no additional liability. Higher/additional rate taxpayers pay the extra.
Top-slicing reliefDivides the gain by the number of years the bond has been held to determine a 'slice'. The slice is added to income to determine the effective marginal rate. Reduces the rate applicable to the full gain.
Offshore bondsNo tax deducted within the fund (gross roll-up). On encashment: full income tax (no 20% credit). But deferral until encashment can be tax-efficient.
Critical Exam Points: (1) The 5% rule is a deferral, not an exemption — tax is eventually due. (2) Chargeable gains are taxed as income, not CGT. (3) Basic rate credit of 20% means UK bonds are grossed up at basic rate. (4) Top-slicing is a relief that may reduce effective rate — it does not exempt the gain.

33. Term Life Assurance Policies

Pure protection — pays a lump sum (or income) on death within a specified term. No investment element. No surrender value (usually).

TypeSum assuredTypical use
Level termFixed throughout termInterest-only mortgage protection; family protection
Decreasing termReduces over time (mirrors repayment mortgage balance)Repayment mortgage protection (cheaper premiums)
Increasing termIncreases each year (e.g., by RPI or fixed %)Inflation protection for family income needs
Convertible termOption to convert to whole-of-life without further medical evidenceClients who may need permanent cover later
Renewable termOption to renew at end of term without new medical evidenceShort-term cover with flexibility
Family Income BenefitPays a regular income (not lump sum) from date of claim to end of termReplace ongoing family income; cheaper than level term
Term vs whole-of-life: Term only pays if death occurs within the term — it is cheaper as there is no certainty of payout. Whole-of-life assurance (covered in Day 09) is certain to pay out eventually — hence higher premiums. Term is the most appropriate recommendation for mortgage protection.

Memorise

ISA Key Numbers
  • Annual ISA limit: £20,000
  • LISA: max £4,000/year; 25% bonus (max £1,000)
  • LISA penalty: 25% of withdrawal; age limit to open: 18–39
  • Junior ISA: £9,000/year; accessible at 18
  • Unused ISA allowance: CANNOT carry forward
Investment Bonds (5% Rule)
  • 5% of original investment per year, deferred not exempt
  • Unused allowance accumulates
  • Chargeable events: death, surrender, excess withdrawal
  • Gains taxed as income (not CGT)
  • 20% basic rate credit; top-slicing may help HR taxpayers
Investment Trust vs OEIC/Unit Trust
  • Investment trust: closed-ended, listed, can gear, discount/premium to NAV
  • OEIC: open-ended, single price, ACD, umbrella structure
  • Unit trust: open-ended, dual price, trustee, COLL rules
Qualifying Policy vs Investment Bond
  • Qualifying: regular premiums, 10-year+ term, sum assured â¥75% premiums â gain tax-FREE
  • Investment bond: single premium, non-qualifying â 5% rule, chargeable events, income tax on gain

Practice Questions

Q1. Marcus, aged 30, contributes £4,000 to his Lifetime ISA in 2024/25. He then withdraws the entire balance to fund a car purchase. Which of the following best describes the outcome?
A. He receives the full balance back including the government bonus — no penalty for withdrawal
B. He pays a 25% penalty on the withdrawal amount, which claws back the bonus AND a portion of his own contributions
C. He pays a 25% penalty only on the government bonus received, not his own contributions
D. He loses the government bonus but receives all his own contributions back in full
Reveal answer
Answer: B. The LISA withdrawal penalty is 25% of the total withdrawal amount (including the bonus). Since the bonus was 25% of his £4,000 = £1,000, his LISA pot was £5,000. The 25% penalty on £5,000 = £1,250. He gets back £5,000 â £1,250 = £3,750 — meaning he loses his £1,000 bonus AND £250 of his own money. A car purchase does not qualify as an exempt reason (only first home up to £450k, age 60+, terminal illness, or death are exempt).
Q2. An investment trust currently trades at a 12% discount to its Net Asset Value (NAV). If the NAV per share is £2.50, at what price are the shares trading?
A. £2.80
B. £2.20
C. £2.50
D. £2.30
Reveal answer
Answer: B — £2.20. A 12% discount means the share price is 12% BELOW the NAV. £2.50 Ã (1 â 0.12) = £2.50 Ã 0.88 = £2.20. At a discount, investors buy £1.00 of underlying assets for £0.88 — potentially attractive if the discount narrows. At a premium the opposite applies (investors pay more than the underlying assets are worth).
Q3. David invested £100,000 in an investment bond 5 years ago. He has taken no withdrawals. He now wishes to withdraw £30,000. What is the maximum he can withdraw without triggering an immediate chargeable event?
A. £5,000 — the annual 5% allowance for the current year only
B. £10,000 — the current year plus one year's carry-forward
C. £25,000 — five years of unused 5% allowances accumulated
D. £30,000 — any withdrawal is allowed without tax
Reveal answer
Answer: C — £25,000. The 5% withdrawal rule allows 5% of the original investment (£100,000 Ã 5% = £5,000) per year of the policy. After 5 years, David has accumulated 5 Ã £5,000 = £25,000 of tax-deferred withdrawal allowance. If he withdraws £30,000, the excess of £5,000 (£30,000 â £25,000) is a partial surrender exceeding the allowance and triggers a chargeable event on that excess.
